At my workplace, we have a lot of customers email us everyday. The manager of the customer support team likes them to receive a response immediately, even if it's not the response they are looking for. So the mailbox has a rule that autoreplies to all incoming emails with a template. So the customers immediately know that we've received the email and will follow it up soon. I had nothing to do with it.

If you know anything about emails, you'll know why this is a bad idea.

A few weeks ago, I get a cry for help forwarded to me. It's from $TEAMLEADER in the customer support team. I am not really IT but I have fixed email problems in the past.

$TEAMLEADER: Flat_hedgehog, we're getting so many emails through from postmaster@<emailprovider>.com. Are our emails to customers with <emailprovider> accounts being rejected? Do <emailprovider> hate us?

I go over to her and have a look at the inbox. Sure enough, we're getting an email from postmaster every 5 minutes, like clockwork. 10:35, 10:40, 10:45... It's a template advising the type of people who need to email postmaster, like how to tell if your IP address has been blacklisted. I go back to my own computer and email postmaster@<emailprovider>.com from my work account and get the same template back, just the once. It's clearly an autoreply. And there was the cause of the problem. Postmaster had originally emailed us to let us know it couldn't deliver a message. We had autoreplied with our "thanks for your email" template and postmaster had autoreplied back, triggering our autoreply again. The only reason we didn't have 10,000 emails is because postmaster emails in batches every 5 minutes, instead of immediately.

The only way to stop a autoreply storm is to turn off one or both autoreplies briefly. I go upstairs and locate $ITMANAGER, who can access the rules on the mailbox. He blusters a bit but does as I ask. It's obvious he has no clue what to do. Back to him later.

I send a nice email to my work group, the customer support work group, local IT and middle management to let everyone know what went wrong. I promise a more permanent fix by close of business. The most obvious solution is to remove our autoreply. I hate autoreplies. The internet hates autoreplies. Why do we have one?

Flat_hedgehog: Can we get rid of the autoreply? It's causing problems and there's no point having it if you can genuinely reply to the customer within the day.

$MANAGER: No! Flat_hedgehog, our customers need to know that we've received their emails! They need to know we care about their emails!

In their defence, they are short staffed and customers may not get a reply that same day. I have to find a different solution. Left alone with a problem that might be his responsibility, $ITMANAGER comes back saying he's found the perfect solution. He's found some software online for £100 that will detect and stop autoreply storms. I go ballistic. We can't spend money on this. It's hard enough getting the licenses on our day-to-day software renewed. No one will give us money for new software that may or may not work.

What I come up with is a compromise. The autoreply will work unless the subject line of the incoming email contains the subject line of our template, which would indicate a reply to our autoreply template, or if the sender of the incoming email contains any of list of key words: postmaster, daemon, bounce, noreply, no-reply, donotreply or do-not-reply, which would indicate an autoreply sender.

I email the same groups to explain the fix. I get some thanks from the customer support team and tumbleweed from everyone else.

TDLR: Don't use an autoreply.
